name: Soy avoidance

lead: Some people avoid soy believing its plant estrogens lower testosterone or feminise men.
A 2020 meta-analysis found no effect of soy or isoflavones on male reproductive hormones in healthy people.

paras: Isoflavones are phytoestrogens that bind estrogen receptors weakly in lab settings; human hormone effects were not found in pooled trials.
Avoidance itself has no described harm in the sources; allergies are the established reason to avoid soy.

lead: Soy avoidance is the practice of cutting soy foods from the diet because of fears that their isoflavones, plant compounds classed as phytoestrogens, lower testosterone, raise estrogen or feminise men. The idea circulates widely in fitness and looksmaxxing communities.

Soy products contain the most isoflavones of any common food group.[1] A 2020 meta-analysis by Reed, Camargo and Messina found that neither soy nor isoflavone intake affected male reproductive hormones, and a 2021 review by Messina and colleagues concluded soyfoods do not warrant classification as endocrine disruptors; a separate 2020 review in Nutrients found insufficient clinical evidence of phytoestrogen effects in humans.[1]

paras: Proponents argue that phytoestrogens mimic estrogen and could suppress male hormones; the article notes fertility effects of phytoestrogens remain under study.[1]

The Linus Pauling Institute reported that intakes above typical Asian diet levels did not change estrogen, testosterone, sperm or semen measures, and found no adverse effects of soy infant formula on growth or reproduction.[1] The American Academy of Pediatrics sees few indications for soy formula over cow's milk formula except specific conditions.[1] Some studies reported isoflavone supplements improved sperm measures, while reviews found no link to male fertility.[1]
Controlled human data are summarised in a 2020 meta-analysis finding no effect of soy or isoflavones on male reproductive hormones in healthy people.[1]
